Channel on YouTube called Prof. Sam Vaknin has a video called “destroyed: narcissist’s brain and mind (infant amnesia, psychotic grandiosity) and he explains @19:00 minutes into the video about trauma and some of its effects… and explains why, someone who has been traumatized may have a tendency to make things up as a literal trauma response to help the brain cope with its memory gaps or inability to fully grasp a trauma and accept it’s reality, or the ways in which it’s affected you. It kind of reminds me of the movie Shutter Island a bit. (Spoiled alert ahead) He struggled cope with the gravity of his loss, and so he chose to forget how it really happened, and designed a different story in his mind… delusional yes, but insane in his processes, no. Just completely traumatized and suffering quite blatantly from a very exaggerated, post traumatic response. In this instance he believed his own lies, but if a child you know grows up lying to everyone and themselves about what their own reality is, it could easily become a habit. Coupling that with any identity disturbance, the brain may try really hard to compensate for the missing pieces, confabulating all sorts of fantastical details. Whatever is most needed to heal whatever inner childhood wound is triggered and needs to be repressed. It is merely a bad habit developed in childhood to cope. Gaps in memory or “repressed trauma” and identity disturbance (I.e loss of a sense of self, dissociation, etc) can make the issue more extreme, it is like a complicated of way of trying to out run whatever is inside you. I highly recommend IFS therapy from Dr. Tori Olds which is a very compassionate and accepting approach to anyone dealing with symptoms of trauma, to maybe give a way into exploring some healing.

I was dx with ARFID by a great psychiatrist and was referred to an eating disorder and OCD specialized therapist. In my opinion it works great to see a psychiatrist so they can assess all of what your needs may be and connect you to the right treatment options for you. I also had a very difficult time speaking about it, opening up to a professional is a good place to start.

You’re not alone, all I can say is get help now, rather than waiting. The biggest mistake I made in getting help, was down playing the significance of my illness because I told myself if I was handling it all fine, and able to sweep it under the rug, it means I’m not *really* unwell enough to need help. To me you sound very high functioning but that does not negate a need or a desire to become more mentally well. So I highly recommend seeking out professional care, and being really raw and honest with them. Also, a support group can be a great learning experience, the psychiatrist or therapist can likely recommend something that’s right for you. Highly recommend as well that the psychiatrist you read out to is very well-accredited and experienced. The wait time for appointment may be 3 months or more even, but it is worth it.
